newsitem.title: UK: Harvey Nichols boss has an eye for a bargain.
newsitem.headline: Harvey Nichols boss has an eye for a bargain.

text.p: Harvey Nichols, the posh London department store where exclusive designer labels fill the racks, is no place for bargain hunters.
But Dickson Poon, the multimillionaire Hong Kong businessman who bought the Knightsbridge shop, knows a good deal when he sees one.

Poon snapped up the classy, but loss-making 180-year old store for 51 million pounds ($83.6 million) in October 1991, in the midst of recession. He floated off 49.9 percent of it just five years later, raising 150 million. Profits in 1995/96 surged 53 percent to 9.2 million pounds.
On Monday when the group unveils results for the past financial year, earnings are predicted to jump again by more than 40 percent to around 13 million pounds.

"They've certainly done a good job," said Steve Davies, retail analyst at Corporate Intelligence. He said the store had been losing out to Knightsbridge neighbour Harrods but had been turned around under Poon's management.

Expansion and refurbishment rapidly transformed Harvey Nichols into one of London's hottest fashion destinations, with exclusive rights to sell top designers such as Givenchy and Dolce & Gabbana couture.
The shop's renaissance was given added momentum by a retail revival which favoured the luxury end of the market, as well as from London's rise as the designer capital of Europe.
Its prime location on the corner of Knightsbridge and exclusive Sloane Street has made Harvey Nichols one of the landmarks of London's high fashion scene.
A favourite of Princess Diana's, the store also received a boost from the British hit comedy series Absolutely Fabulous, whose lead characters loved to go on spending binges at Harvey Nicks.
The group has branched out into restaurants, opening up in the Oxo Tower on London's south bank and last October opened its first store outside London in the northern city of Leeds.
Leeds was seen as a risky venture by some sophisticated southerners, but has proved a big draw for high-income fashion lovers in the north of England, analysts said.
"They even had to close the doors at times because the demand was so great," said one analyst.
At least two more shops are planned outside the capital, possibly in Manchester and Glasgow.
Poon's timing of both the acquisition and flotation was well judged. "He bought at the bottom and probably sold at the top," said Richard Hyman of retail consultants Verdict.
Harvey Nichols' shares have turned in a sparkling performance since the flotation. But perceptions that the company's hectic growth might be slackening have taken the stock from its highs.
At midday Thursday, the stock was half a pence down at 302 1/2 pence, down from a high of 350 pence, but still well up on the flotation price of 270.
"It's all still quite exciting," said one retail analyst, "but since the Leeds opening things seemed to have slowed down and there's been no more news on new store openings."
Poon, 40, head of Hong Kong based Dickson Concepts, is no stranger to luxury designer labels.

He comes from a wealthy Hong Kong family and was educated in Britain and the United States. But he went his own way and built up his Dickson Concepts empire from a single watch and jewellery store which opened in 1980 into a multimillion dollar business marketing top international brands like Ralph Lauren and Escada. Interim profits in December increased five-fold to around HK$833 million.

He owns a white Bentley and has homes in Hong Kong, London and Los Angeles and is already on his third marriage. His second wife Michelle Yeoh, Miss Malaysia 1983, has since become one of Asia's top paid actresses.

In 1987 he bought French pen and cigarette lighter firm S.T. Dupont and a year ago acquired an 85 percent stake in upmarket Chinese department store group Hong Kong Seibu Enterprise Co for HK$180 million.
His latest move is an attempt to enter the luxury goods market in the United States by buying Barney's Inc, the famous New York store, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection last year.

Dickson Concepts, with HK$1.3 billion in the bank, had offered to buy Barney's for $240 million, but the bid was rejected as too low. U.S. retailers Neiman Marcus Group Inc Saks Holdings Inc are seen as rival bidders, but analysts say Poon is unlikely to be drawn into a bidding war. ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
